topicName: Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) Architecture and CNI
content: [{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) Architecture and CNI Technical Tutorial"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"This tutorial covers the architectural foundations of Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) and dives deep into Container Network Interface (CNI) plug-in options. Understanding these components is critical for designing scalable, secure, and high-performance Kubernetes deployments on Microsoft Azure."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"1. AKS Core Architecture"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"An AKS cluster is split into two primary components: the control plane, managed entirely by Azure, and the worker nodes, managed by the user within their subscription."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Control Plane: Provided as a managed service by Azure, handling the API server, etcd, scheduler, and controller manager. It is abstracted and highly available."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Node Pools: Virtual machines running Kubernetes node components (kubelet, kube-proxy, container runtime) mapped to user resource groups."},{"order":7,"type":"subheading","text":"2. Azure CNI vs. Kubenet"},{"order":8,"type":"paragraph","text":"Networking in AKS is driven by the CNI plug-in. Azure offers two primary networking models: Kubenet (basic) and Azure CNI (advanced)."},{"order":9,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Kubenet: Nodes get IP addresses from the Azure Virtual Network (VNet). Pods get IP addresses from a logical address space routed via NAT, requiring user-defined routes (UDR)."},{"order":10,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Azure CNI: Every pod receives an IP address directly from the Azure VNet, enabling flat networking where pods can communicate directly with other services in the VNet."},{"order":11,"type":"subheading","text":"3. Provisioning an AKS Cluster with Azure CNI"},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"The following Azure CLI script deploys an AKS cluster using Azure CNI. Ensure you have pre-created your resource group and VNet subnet."},{"order":13,"type":"code","text":"az aks create --resource-group \"myResourceGroup\" --name \"myAKSCluster\" --node-count 3 --network-plugin azure --vnet-subnet-id \"/subscriptions/<sub-id>/resourceGroups/myRG/providers/Microsoft.Network/virtualNetworks/myVnet/subnets/mySubnet\" --generate-ssh-keys"},{"order":14,"type":"subheading","text":"4. IP Address Planning and Scaling"},{"order":15,"type":"paragraph","text":"When using Azure CNI, IP exhaustion is a major architectural consideration because every pod consumes a VNet IP address. Careful subnet sizing is mandatory."},{"order":16,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Max Pods per Node: You can limit the maximum number of pods per node (default is 30) to control VNet IP allocation."},{"order":17,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Dynamic IP Allocation: Newer configurations allow Azure CNI to use a secondary subnet for pod IPs, decoupling node scaling limits from pod IP consumption."},{"order":18,"type":"subheading","text":"Conclusion"},{"order":19,"type":"paragraph","text":"Choosing the right CNI and understanding AKS architecture ensures optimal cluster performance, security boundaries, and enterprise readiness on Microsoft Azure."}]
